title: Policy as Datalog, with derivations
objective: Write the three read rules as Datalog over W0, generate the access matrix, and justify an allowed cell by its derivation and a denied cell rule by rule.

blocks.md: In S7.L1 you read a policy. Now you write one, and you make it explain itself.

choice.prompt: The engine says dana may read contract. Which justification is complete?

options.text: Rule 2 on dana's share of contract, with no revocation derivable.
options.why: Every premise of the rule instance is accounted for.

options.text: Birch lets Acme users read its documents, by rule 3.
options.why: There is no tenant-level grant in the rules.

blocks.md:
A worked example first. Rule 1 reads: `canread(u, d) :- member(u, t, _), owns(t, d).` User u may read document d if u is a member of some team t, in any role (the `_` ignores it), and t owns d. The variable `t` joins the two premises, so it must be one team in both.

Rules 2 and 3 have the same shape. Rule 2 adds a negated premise, `!revoked(d, u)`. Soufflé's rules page sets two conditions for negation: a negated literal binds no variable, so `d` and `u` must already appear in a positive premise, and the program must be stratifiable, with no relation depending on its own negation through a cycle. Run all three rules on W0.

blocks.direction: Query asks: which (user, document) pairs are derivable under rules 1 to 3? The cell draws `canread` as the access matrix.

code.text:
.decl member(u: symbol, t: symbol, r: symbol)
.decl owns(t: symbol, d: symbol)
.decl share_user(d: symbol, u: symbol)
.decl share_team(d: symbol, t: symbol)
.decl revoked(d: symbol, u: symbol)
.decl canread(u: symbol, d: symbol)
.output canread

member("dana", "payments", "editor").  member("frank", "growth", "viewer").
member("gia", "legal", "admin").       member("hal", "legal", "viewer").
owns("payments", "q3-plan").  owns("growth", "roadmap").
owns("legal", "contract").    owns("legal", "layoffs-memo").
share_user("contract", "dana").
share_team("roadmap", "payments").

// rule 1: a member of the owning team
canread(u, d) :- member(u, t, _), owns(t, d).
// rule 2: shared with the user, and not revoked
canread(u, d) :- share_user(d, u), !revoked(d, u).
// rule 3: shared with one of the user's teams
canread(u, d) :- member(u, t, _), share_team(d, t).

options.text: None: the share is still there.
options.why: The revocation removes rule 2's other premise.
dana is not in Legal, and contract has no team share.

blocks.after: You changed one fact, and the engine recomputed every consequence. Rules and facts stay separate.

choice.prompt: Translate: "Editors of the owning team may read a document, and so may anyone it is shared with, unless that share is revoked." Which rules say it?

options.text: `canread(u, d) :- member(u, t, "editor"), owns(t, d).` and `canread(u, d) :- share_user(d, u), !revoked(d, u).`
options.why: Two ways in, each with its own premises, and the revocation guards the share.

options.text: `canread(u, d) :- member(u, t, "editor"), owns(t, d).` and `canread(u, d) :- share_user(d, u).`
options.why: The second rule ignores revocations, so a revoked share still allows the read.

options.text: `canread(u, d) :- member(u, t, "editor"), owns(t, d), share_user(d, u), !revoked(d, u).`
options.why: One rule joins the two ways in, so it demands both at once.

blocks.md: An allowed cell has a derivation: a tree whose leaves are facts and whose nodes are rule instances. Soufflé prints trees of minimal height. A denied cell has no tree, because nothing derived it. To justify a denial you go through the rules and name, for each, the first premise that finds no match. Soufflé's provenance page says it cannot generate explanations for non-existence automatically.

blocks.direction: Query asks: explain `canread("dana", "contract")` with a derivation, and `canread("frank", "contract")` rule by rule.

code.text:
.decl member(u: symbol, t: symbol, r: symbol)
.decl owns(t: symbol, d: symbol)
.decl share_user(d: symbol, u: symbol)
.decl share_team(d: symbol, t: symbol)
.decl revoked(d: symbol, u: symbol)
.decl canread(u: symbol, d: symbol)
.output canread

member("dana", "payments", "editor").  member("frank", "growth", "viewer").
member("gia", "legal", "admin").       member("hal", "legal", "viewer").
owns("payments", "q3-plan").  owns("growth", "roadmap").
owns("legal", "contract").    owns("legal", "layoffs-memo").
share_user("contract", "dana").
share_team("roadmap", "payments").

canread(u, d) :- member(u, t, _), owns(t, d).
canread(u, d) :- share_user(d, u), !revoked(d, u).
canread(u, d) :- member(u, t, _), share_team(d, t).

call.prompt: Can a denial be justified by one tree, the way an allowance can?

options.why: Absence is not a fact, so it has no proof tree.
A denial says no instance of any rule applies, so you go rule by rule.

blocks.after: For dana and contract, Soufflé prints a one-leaf tree: `share_user("contract", "dana")` under the share rule, which it labels `R3` by its own numbering. The tree leaves out the negated premise, so a complete justification adds that `revoked("contract", "dana")` is not derivable. For frank and contract it prints `Tuple not found` {{run:RUN-datalog-matrix}}. For frank and contract, rule 1 matches frank's team, but Growth does not own contract. Rule 2 finds no share to frank. Rule 3 finds contract shared with no team. Three rules, three first failures.

choice.prompt: Why can't frank read contract? Pick the complete account.

options.text: No rule applies: frank fails a premise of rule 1, rule 2 and rule 3.
options.why: Each rule is accounted for by its first failing premise.

options.text: Tenants: frank is in Acme and contract belongs to Birch, so they differ.
options.why: No rule mentions tenants, and a share could still cross that boundary.

options.text: Rule 2 fails: contract is revoked for frank, and the others do not matter.
options.why: Nothing is revoked for frank; rule 2 fails because no share names him.
The variable `t` must be one team in both premises, and dana's team does not own roadmap.
dana is on Payments and roadmap is shared with Payments, so every premise is a fact.
No fact shares roadmap with dana as a user, so the rule has no instance.

blocks.title: Twin
blocks.md: Cedar's Lean model is an executable specification, with properties such as default deny and "forbid trumps permit" checked in Lean. It is the first of Cedar's three layers of evidence, described in the [Cedar paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.04651). Pins: {{run:RUN-twin-pins}}.

A pin is the commit a ref pointed to when ls-remote read it; read_at is that instant. The record is stale 60 days after its started_at and is refreshed by re-running the commands in argv.

git ls-remote was first run with several ref patterns per command (HEAD plus refs/tags/... or refs/heads/...); for leanprover/lean4 and postgres/postgres that printed nothing with exit 0. The recorded run uses one pattern per command; the pin for lean4 tags and PR 14577 uses a trailing * pattern, and every matching ref is kept in refs.

refs/pull/14577/merge is not advertised; only refs/pull/14577/head is. The v4.35.0 tag points at eb6cafb7290e8bd5f2937522d8d804f58f02bafc, the commit the bench image's Lean prints in its version string.

Twin cards that name no git repository are not pinned here: Stripe's "Idempotent requests" API page, the Zanzibar paper (USENIX ATC 2019), Jepsen's PostgreSQL 12.3 analysis, the arXiv papers on Cedar and CCF, SymCert (FMCAD 2026) and the AWS Automated Reasoning checks pages. Each card states its own read date.
Isabelle is developed in Mercurial; the pin is from its GitHub mirror, isabelle-prover/mirror-isabelle.
input sha256 for each command is the SHA-256 of the lines it printed, joined by newlines with a trailing newline.
